prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which opened a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and the optical lattice clock third, and having read all eight ballots I now propose the clock as the preferred prize. It is the only shortlisted candidate that five of eight colleagues place in their top three, two of them at rank 1, and it is supported by members from atomic physics (Lindroth), quantum physics (Johansson), precision measurement (Kroll) and instrumentation (Olsson). As an instrument builder I value it for the reason the others give: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea combined with Ye's group taking systematic uncertainty to the 1e-18 level is a new measurement capability, not just a better number. It enables tests of relativistic time dilation over millimetres, searches for varying constants and dark-matter signatures, and a path to redefining the second. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) have reproduced and surpassed the early results, which is exactly the independent confirmation I ask for. The two-name credit is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and the invention was not covered by the 2005 comb prize or the 2012 ion-control prize. Recognition looks timely.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are overlap and attribution at the edges. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch) provided the comb that reads out optical clocks and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) covered quantum control of single ions, which also underlies the best ion clocks, so some will say the field is already honoured. Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Sterr and the NIST and PTB groups made essential parallel or later contributions, and a two-person prize leaves them out. The SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue we should wait for that story to finish. Finally, it is a technology-heavy topic and the physics 'discovery' content is mostly what the clock will reveal later, not yet an observed new phenomenon. I take these seriously, but none of them undermines the invention itself.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks the clock first and asks whether we should wait for the SI redefinition of the second to complete the story.
responses.response: I do not think we should wait. The prize rewards the invention and its demonstrated performance, which are already confirmed by several independent laboratories and international clock comparisons. Tying the prize to a metrological decision by the CGPM would make our timing depend on a process we do not control. I do agree with your point that Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr and the ion-clock lineage are a real attribution boundary. I would draw the line at the invention (Katori) and its leading realisation at record accuracy and in many-body regimes (Ye), and say so in the citation.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery with ATLAS and CMS first, as the clearest experimental clue in modern fundamental physics and the experimental half left over from 2013.
responses.response: I agree on importance and maturity and I ranked it fifth only because of attribution, not merit. Your trio (Gianotti, Della Negra, Virdee) differs from Lindroth's and mine (Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee), and Olsson's (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni): three of us nominate three different trios from the same four names. That spread shows that any three-person cut drops a founder of one experiment and will be read as unfair to a collaboration of thousands. Unless you can argue for a principled criterion, for example spokespersons at the time of discovery, I would rather not make that the committee's first choice this year. I would be glad to be persuaded otherwise if the colleagues with particle-physics expertise find a defensible rule.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a new state of matter with a clean theory-and-experiment trio.
responses.response: I find the physics compelling but I rely on you for condensed matter. My worry is the one Lindroth, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson also raise: the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional topological insulators, sit outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Molenkamp's experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, not the graphene model, so the experimental credit and the theory credit are not for the same system. If that can be handled with a citation focused on the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation, I could support it as the second prize choice, but I would want a convincing answer on the attribution before putting it ahead of the clock.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks the clock first as a measurement advance that opens new observational regimes, with Katori and Ye a clean and fair configuration.
responses.response: I agree with both the scientific and the attribution argument. I would add a qualification: Ye's contribution includes the many-body and spin-exchange understanding that made the lattice clock reach 1e-18, so the citation should name the invention and the development together, not only the magic-wavelength idea. This also addresses the concern that Katori alone would leave the performance story out.

responses.point: Goran Johansson ranks circuit QED first and the clock second, and notes that a cQED prize would be complementary to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
responses.response: I respect that and I note that you flag your own proximity to the community. My hesitation is timing and attribution rather than quality: returning to superconducting circuits one year after 2025 will be read as a repeat, and Girvin and Huang are missing from the Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf trio. Since you also put the clock second, I see the clock as the candidate on which we agree most, and I would suggest we use the next round to test whether cQED is better held for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a two-person prize for the lattice clock leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr and other laboratories that contributed, or wants a different credit boundary.
Whether overlap with the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (ion control) prizes weakens the novelty case for the clock.
Whether IceCube (my own first choice) is mature enough in source identification, and how to credit AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers beyond Halzen and Karle.
Whether any three-person cut of the four ATLAS and CMS leaders can be defended; I have no principled rule and rely on particle-physics colleagues.
My assessment of the quantum-matter candidates (topological insulators, twisted bilayer graphene, optical-lattice simulation, circuit QED) depends on colleagues' expertise, which is outside mine.
statement.conflict_note: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and at KTH; none of these is part of IceCube, EHT or the optical lattice clock, so no specific conflict is apparent for the preferred candidate. For IceCube, my Fermi-LAT membership overlaps with multi-messenger follow-up of TXS 0506+056 in the wider community, which is a field-proximity tie but not a personal or institutional connection to the credited names. As Chair I also have no personal connection to Katori or Ye apparent from my profile.
